claims.text: Atomic-scale kinetics during rapid heating and cooling are the dominant factor controlling crystal-structure selection in noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Rapid processing can prevent atoms from fully diffusing.
Insufficient diffusion during rapid processing freezes in a metastable single-phase structure.
An intermediate-temperature dwell increases atomic diffusion before final cooling.
The degree of atomic diffusion controls the uniformity of the elemental distribution.
The degree of atomic diffusion determines whether the alloy remains a metastable single phase or develops segregation and secondary phases.
Increased atomic mobility during the dwell allows constituent elements to segregate and rearrange toward their equilibrium phases.
Relative to rapid heating and cooling, an intermediate dwell should increase phase separation or secondary-phase formation.
The intermediate dwell may alter nanoparticle morphology relative to the rapid-processing baseline.
Rapid heating and cooling typically yield a metastable single-phase solid solution in these multielement nanoparticles.
The proposed dwell effect applies near compositional and thermodynamic boundaries where kinetic constraints dominate over equilibrium mixing enthalpies.
For compositions with a very strong thermodynamic driving force for single-phase stability, the dwell period should have little effect.
The dwell time and temperature required to trigger measurable segregation are system-dependent and require experimental calibration.
